newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: North Afghan leader promises Islamic law.
newsitem.headline: North Afghan leader promises Islamic law.

text.p: General Abdul Malik, the opposition military leader whose mutiny toppled Afghan warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum this weekend, promised a new Islamic order in the north.
"There will be Islamic Shariah (law) in the north," Malik, an ethnic Uzbek, told a news conference in Mazar-i-Sharif, one day after his troops swept in the northern capital.
"I am a son of Islam, my ancestors were Moslems and I was not educated at Moscow as Dostum was," he said in response to a question about his Islamic credentials.

Malik, who was Dostum's deputy until he staged his revolt last Monday in favour of the purist Islamic Taleban movement, said an Islamic Afghanistan would not threaten Russia or Central Asian republics on its northern frontier.

"We don't want to attack Russia," he said. "We want the Central Asian countries to be independent and separate from the (former) Soviet Union. We want Islam, but it is up to the people in those countries."
Moscow has very strong concerns that Taleban's militancy might spread beyond Afghanistan's borders.

Malik asked for international recognition of the "Islamic government of Afghanistan," -- so far denied to the Taleban administration in Kabul -- and urged "all countries, especially the United States, to help people of Afghanistan develop."
The Taleban, who control most of Afghanistan, have imposed strict Islamic rules, and have prevented most women and girls from going to school.
They have enforced harsh punishments, amputations for theft, ordered men to grow beards and prohibited music and dancing and videos and many other pastimes.
Malik, indicating that Shariah law would also apply in the north, said religious scholars would decide the details.

"In the past there was co-education for boys and girls, which is illegal in the eyes of Islam," he said, adding that girls should not expect to receive education until economic conditions allowed the building of segregated facilities.

Under Dostum, who fought for the former communist regime and kept control of the north after helping Moslem guerrillas capture Kabul in 1992, life in Mazar-i-Sharif was relatively liberal. Girls could go to school, women could work, no Islamic dress code was enforced and even alcohol could be obtained.
Malik, who is clean shaven apart from a moustache, said his troops were not under Taleban command but there was no difference between them and the Taleban forces.

However, the turban-clad general urged the Taleban's remaining opponents -- ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani, his military chief Ahmed Shah Masood and Shi'ite Moslem faction leader Karim Khalili -- to stop fighting and negotiate.
"We have asked them to join us in the name of God," he said. "Continuing to fight will not be in their interest. It's best to be all together under the flag of Islam."
Malik, seated beneath the portrait of his older brother Rasul Pahlivan, a senior Dostum commander assassinated last year, said all Dostum's troops have now joined him.
"We don't want to fight," he said. "We want all other parties to join in a peace project under Shariah law."
